For a first look that stays on your machine, they stay out of the way. Two session hooks come with them. items.title: Show HN: WOML – A markup language for building workflows and AI agents
items.story_key: story|title:woml a markup language for building workflows and ai agents
items.content_excerpt: Readable markup for structure. JavaScript for logic. A durable runtime for execution. WOML is an open-source, code-first language and runtime for building automated workflows, backend applications, and AI agents. Describe the process in readable, HTML-inspired markup, use JavaScript for logic, and connect the APIs, services, databases, local tools, and infrastructure involved. The workflow source is the program, its readable architecture, and its execution policy. It can live in Git, move through pull requests and CI, and run locally or on infrastructure you control. Start with one workflow for a local task or webhook. As the work grows, extract reusable modules, call or start other workflows, publish events, and operate the result as a coordinated system without changing its underlying model. Native engines are selected automatically for supported macOS, Linux, and Windows systems. You do not need to install the platform packages or configure a database manually. WOML keeps the automation active and prints its webhook URL together with a generated curl command. Trigger it from another terminal: Use auth="none" only for local development. Configure authenticated webhooks before exposing an endpoint outside a trusted environment. WOML presents each run as an organized, colored terminal report. You will see output like this: The exact run ID and timings will differ. Press Ctrl + C to stop the active workflow host. Provider examples require their documented credentials. Browse the complete example catalog for webhooks, schedules, intervals, internal events, databases, storage, cache, lifecycle, retries, communication providers, and production deployment. A WOML project can begin with one file and grow into a system of focused workflows and modules. Workflows can call another workflow and wait for its result, start independent work in the background, or publish events that other workflows consume. Create a project with workflow discovery and operator-owned configuration already in place: The generated workflow.json keeps workflow discovery, policies, reviewers, and execution targets reviewable while secret values remain outside source control. The same project model supports local execution, durable artifacts and waits, rich approvals, infrastructure policies, streamed output, OpenTelemetry, and authenticated remote targets. Remote work never silently falls back to the coordinator. Read the project manifest reference , follow the infrastructure-agent tutorial

items.story_key: story|title:bugtape production bugs your coding agent can read and fix over mcp
items.content_excerpt: Error tracking for your coding agent. Replay, requests, console and stack, captured before anyone files a ticket. The steps, the failed request, the console and the stack, grouped into one issue. Run one command in your app’s repository. It creates or selects your project and gives you the install steps. Sign in and approve access in your browser. Your agent connects over MCP. Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ChatGPT, Grok and any HTTP MCP client. Browser replay is for web apps. Node.js and Python capture server error context. Swift is a handled-error alpha, with no fatal-crash or native-replay support. What a report holds depends on capture settings and the event. Replay is reconstructed page activity, not a video. Replay can be unavailable. Request and response bodies are not captured. A stack is evidence, not a confirmed cause. Inputs are masked by default. Visible page text can still be recorded; strict mode masks page text too. Music: Neon by Scott Buckley · CC BY 4.0 (edited). Keyboard: Keychron V1 typing by C40115 · CC BY 4.0 (edited). No. With the browser SDK installed, supported errors and failed requests can create reports automatically. Capture settings and rate limits apply. Users can also submit a report. BugTape captures and shares evidence. Your authorized coding agent can investigate and propose a change. You review it. An agent response or linked pull request does not prove the fix works. One project, three members, 100 new issues and 150 credits a month, with seven-day event retention. No credit card. See what credits cover. The demo captures a real failure locally in your browser tab. It does not send a report to BugTape or dispatch an agent. Install the SDK in your app to capture your own reports. Yes. npx -y bugtape --help prints the CLI and does not sign you in. The live demo runs in your browser and sends nothing. The demo MCP at https://app.bugtape.ai/demo/mcp needs no sign-in. Your own workspace needs one. No. It keeps a short buffer in the browser and sends that buffer with a supported error or a user report.

items.content_excerpt: NVIDIA RTX Spark powers thin and light laptops built for everything that developers, creators and gamers do. RTX Spark laptops are now available from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. These powerful systems combine an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU in a single superchip with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That puts the NVIDIA CUDA platform, RTX graphics and the capabilities of a personal AI supercomputer inside premium Windows laptops built to go anywhere. Introduced today, NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a new, open weight speech model that turns recorded conversations into useful information. Instead of needing multiple models for transcription, speaker labels and translation, developers can use one promptable model that handles all three, plus questions about the audio. It transcribes 40 languages, including seven Indic languages. Developers guide the model with plain-language prompts. For example, for a single recorded meeting, users can ask it to: Prompts can also include product terms and formatting conventions, which helps the model handle specialized vocabulary in fields like healthcare, financial services and customer service. Because the weights are open, developers can choose where audio is processed, from a desktop to the cloud. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks No. 1 on the Hugging Face Open ASR and No. 2 among open weight models on Artificial Analysis — delivering leading accuracy with approximately 4.3 billion active parameters, 80% fewer than the No. 1 open weight model, making high-quality, intelligent transcription more practical on local hardware. It’s available today on Hugging Face in the BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 formats, and offers flexible deployment options for developers with support on NVIDIA RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, Jetson AGX Thor devices and GeForce RTX 5090 GPUs. Developers can deploy NVFP4 versions through NeMo-Speech.cpp or vLLM. On RTX Spark, users can have long-running agents working alongside their favorite applications. Both share the system’s GPU compute, and the right balance of resources depends on what matters to users at that moment. With the new resource management feature in NVIDIA App , users can now choose how GPU resources are shared. They can prioritize their foreground app for the best performance, or give their background-running agent more resources to get work done faster. items.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt
items.story_key: model:nemotron|ver:3.5|title:nvidia nemotron 3 5 transcribe and granary v2 intelligent multilingual transcrip
items.content_excerpt: A transcript can capture every spoken word and still leave users or applications wondering who said what, how to translate it, or how to format domain-specific jargon. Multilingual calls, fast-paced meetings, and medical dictation each need different output: a translation, speaker labels, or correctly spelled medical terms. NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is an open-weight, promptable model that turns recorded speech into useful text, now available on Hugging Face and ModelScope . It brings transcription, speaker attribution (diarization), translation, and audio question answering into one checkpoint: it transcribes 40 languages, translates 31 of them to or from English, and attributes speakers in 13. It handles recordings up to an hour long and labels up to eight speakers. Developers can guide output with natural language, choose where their audio is processed, and adapt recognition to domain vocabulary and accents. Transcribe is first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard for English and sits on Artificial Analysis ’s accuracy–active-parameter frontier. For speaker attribution, it posts the lowest error rate on David AI’s 21-language diarization leaderboard and ranks first in VoiceArena’s 14-system comparison . It runs on a single NVIDIA GPU, from DGX Spark to Blackwell data-center systems. Granary v2’s multilingual data (available on Hugging Face and ModelScope ) and reusable curation pipeline, together with NeMo Speech fine-tuning tools , extend prompt-level control to training: developers can define the written form they need and adapt the model to the speech their applications encounter. In a medical case study , fine-tuning cut word error rate (WER) on held-out speakers by 45.8% relative to the best prompt. The same checkpoint can turn one meeting recording into different outputs, depending on the instruction: Experience the model in action in the video below, where it tackles a classic scene from the 1940 screwball comedy His Girl Friday—a film famous for its rapid-fire, heavily overlapping dialogue. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe captions a scene from His Girl Friday (1940) and labels speakers, including overlapping dialogue. For unfamiliar terms, try context before training. In a healthcare setting, for example: Transcribe this medical discussion in the original language. Possible terms: HbA1c, metformin. Use these terms only when supported by the audio. items.title: MoI-Bench: A Benchmark for Image Generation and Editing on Mobile Devices
items.summary: Developing on-device image models requires considering practical user needs, task types and device resource constraints. However, existing benchmarks provide limited guidance on identifying capability gaps between on-device models and server-side models. We introduce MoI-Bench, a benchmark grounded in mobile user needs, comprising 64 subtasks and 1150 samples. It defines 16 operations, such as removal and replacement, and eight visual target categories covering content such as portraits and text. These form two orthogonal axes whose applicable combinations define specific tasks, such as removing facial makeup. To better guide model improvement, we further propose MoI-Eval, which introduces task-specific criteria covering instruction following, visual quality and detail preservation. We further construct sample-level evaluation questions and aggregate their scores into overall quality and capability profiles along the operation, target and criteria axes. We evaluate representative on-device and server-side models and measure mobile deployment costs. Results show that this decoupled Operation x Target design provides finer-grained guidance for improving compact models. For example, it highlights the need to prioritize specific capability gaps (e.g., text-replacement) over broad application-level goals (e.g., improving text editing). Unlike conventional benchmarks that rank models using a single score, we introduce a two-dimensional Quality-Deployability capability map to assess models for practical mobile use. The map shows that current on-device models can achieve efficient generation or editing but expanding their task coverage deserves greater attention than further improving deployment efficiency. Further progress requires improving editing quality, particularly identity preservation and text rendering, while broadening task coverage.

items.title: Evaluating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks
items.summary: As frontier language models grow increasingly capable and autonomous, independent third-party evaluations are critical for characterizing their systemic safety risks. While closed-source releases are routinely accompanied by comprehensive system cards, open-weight models receive less scrutiny regarding frontier risks. To address this gap, we present an independent safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, the latest version of V4.1 Flash that departs from V4 with a new architecture, scaled-up training, and strong agentic capabilities. Drawing on the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, we evaluate the model across 34 benchmarks, including 5 in-house suites, spanning evaluation integrity, loss of control, and harmful manipulation. Conforming to the AEF-1 standard, we compare V4.1 Flash-1017 against V4.1 Flash, earlier DeepSeek V4 models, and leading closed-source systems (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash). Overall, V4.1 Flash-1017 shows substantial safety improvements over the V4 generation and approaches or matches leading closed-source baselines on several dimensions, while still exhibiting notable behaviors that warrant continued attention. Building on our findings, we highlight three key observations and recommendations. First, because safety can shift and even regress across minor updates, developers should integrate safety evaluation into incremental releases. Second, as final-turn outputs and end-state checks alone cannot reliably detect loss-of-control behaviors, deployments require process-level observability across both reasoning traces and action logs. Third, because public benchmarks elicit strong evaluation awareness and face data contamination risks, developing private benchmarks is essential for trustworthy frontier evaluation.

items.title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?
items.summary: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.
